Thus my Crystal Lake journey comes to an end (at least until October). I don't know if I just have Stockholm syndrome or if it was just anti-remake culture that was prevalent when I first watched this, but this movie isn't really that bad. It's still pretty mediocre, it's definitely not an Evil Dead (2013) situation, but in comparison to the following year's Nightmare On Elm Street reinvention, it might as well as be a masterpiece. This film has a real nasty edge with some properly gnarly gore, which does give it its own identity. It kinda surprises me that this is the only outing, which utilises a bear trap, especially because Part 2 sets up that Crystal Lake is bear country, however it does   lead to delightfully horrific results. I'm sure a lot of this is due to the filmmakers wanting to compete with the "torture porn" craze of the time, yet they do manage to hold their own well enough. The unfortunate over side to the grossness coin, it's how much aggressively juvenile misogyny is on display, leering at its female characters in a way only a Micheal Bay produced flick can. Similarly, the American Pie style sex comedy (outside of a few jokes) feels very tired and just unnecessarily unpleasant. The characters are a bit of a nothing burger, although not in a way significantly different than most entries and there's a few good performances scattered in. At first glance, the idea of combining story elements from the first four installments into one narrative sounds like a recipe for disaster, yet those movies are either a bit repetitive or rather simple, that it actually kind of works. The script wasn't gonna awards, the dialogue is far too clunky and there are dumb character decisions and contrivances galore, but some thought clearly went into it. Overall, if you stayed away from this because it's a 2000s horror remake, first of all... Fair. Nonetheless, you can do much much worse.

Not the worst, but completely missing the charm of the other Friday the 13th movies. The franchise was much better when it wasn’t taking itself seriously. And this movie takes itself way too seriously. The movie is also padded out with a lot of sex scenes, and I know it’s Friday the 13th, but if you want sex scenes you can just watch porn. I want to watch a decent movie. Jason is also completely out of character. He doesn’t have the same mannerisms in the other movies, and he kidnaps a woman which doesn’t really match his character (he typically murders teens, rather than kidnapping people). The characters are all just stereotypes (including a black comic relief character, a trope that pisses me off) and it’s hard to feel invested in anything they do. Overall this movie is better than Friday the 13th part four, but I would not recommend this movie to anyone with a functioning brain. Unless you are a die hard fan who is a completionist, then you might be marginally entertained if you can turn you brain off.

So here's the thing, most Friday the 13th films are average. As a series, it doesn't have incredible lows like The Curse of Muchael Myeys or Freddy's Dead, nor the spectacular rebounds like H20 or New Nightmare. It is a series that has remained consistently okay. And that's more or less what this is, another okay entry in the Friday the 13th series. It has all the sex and violence that you expect—actually, a bit more sex than you'd expect for 2009—but doesn't really do much to change up the formula. Ironically, not changing the formula is probably this movie's biggest strength. It's the 12th Friday the 13th movie, and it feels like a Friday the 13th movie. There are some changes that work, some that don't, but overall just an average slasher with a handful of memorable scenes makes for a fairly enjoyable experience if that's your thing. Which weirdly makes it possibly the best of the major horror franchise reboots. Friday the 13th never had the subtext of The Texas Chain Saw Massacre, the quiet suspense of Halloween, or the playful creativity of Evil Dead or A Nightmare on Elm Street. To put it bluntly, there just wasn't really much to fuck up.

I don't think this quite reaches the heights of the best sequels, but it's undeniably a reboot that fundamentally understands the task at hand, and arguably the superior of both Marcus Nispel's 00's horror remakes. Essentially a smooshed-together rendition of the first four original films into a new narrative remix of sorts, after a bit of a ropey opening it skips straight to the good stuff, barrels through the mythology, and gives us Derek Mears' Jason absolutely ruling as a considerably more driven and vicious take on the Hockey Masked killer. I don't really buy the criticisms that it's "too horny", since that promiscuity and lure is kind of part and parcel with the series and its own bizarre detours. The final stretch loses some of the momentum that makes the opening hour such a blast, but the pacing overall is quite relentless, the kills are inventive and nasty, and it's packed with enough of why this series became an institution in the first place. It's a shame it never really spawned anything more, and I look forward to the day we finally get another one of these. Maybe Damien Leone would be a good shout?

Honestly a pretty good adaptation of Friday the 13th. It takes inspiration mainly from the first three films in the series and translates it into a more modern, easily digestible version of the original movies. Also, the teenagers are pretty good, even if a bit one-dimensional, which is arguably appropriate. Aesthetically not the exact same, but it still looks good and has a distinct identity of its own. The teens are fairly decent this time around. They aren't great characters or anything, still lack depth, but they are at least fun to watch for the most part. It certainly helps that Jared Padalecki is in this movie, as he is the most interesting character besides Jason himself. He is searching for his sister, who plays the role of Ginny from Part 2, confusing Jason as his dead mother. Because of this, he kidnaps her and keeps her in tunnels beneath the camp, a new addition to the remake. Speaking of, Jason is portrayed quite well. This time, he is HAULING through the whole movie. I enjoy when Jason walks casually towards his victims, but seeing him sprint full speed is pretty scary too. He starts with the baghead from Part 2 and eventually gets the hockey mask from Part 3, found in a random barn. He also has some pretty brutal and efficient kills. I do wish the climax ended with him fully going into the woodchipper, or at least had an axe in his head to create that iconic top-right chip on the mask. Overall, not bad! It's a different story and a different kind of Jason. Definitely not a replacement, but a good interpretation. With this viewing, my Friday the 13th marathon is complete, aside from Freddy vs. Jason, which I plan to watch when I marathon the Nightmare movies. So, that will be coming soon!

Se você tirar o filtro da nostalgia, percebe que este remake entende Sexta-Feira 13 melhor do que boa parte das continuações. Não tenta transformar Jason em um ícone filosófico nem inventar um trauma geracional; só lembra que ele é um cara enorme de máscara cuja principal função é punir gente que acha uma cabana isolada um bom lugar para passar o fim de semana. O Jason do Derek Mears é praticamente o Anton Chigurh dos slashers: paciente, eficiente e inevitável. Enquanto o elenco parece ter saído de um catálogo de comerciais da Abercrombie dos anos 2000, ele faz de Crystal Lake um roguelike: entrou na floresta, morreu, tenta de novo. É engraçado ver como esse filme foi tratado como heresia em 2009 e hoje parece um dos remakes de terror mais honestos da época. Depois de uma década de "terror elevado", às vezes tudo o que eu quero é um sujeito de 2 metros distribuindo machadadas sem precisar representar um trauma intergeracional. Cinema? Talvez não. Entretenimento? Com certeza. E, convenhamos, se você assiste Sexta-Feira 13 esperando a complexidade de Persona, o problema nunca foi o filme.

Looking at the Rotten Tomatoes score and other reviews for this Friday The 13th remake, it seems like most people pretty much hated it. But I actually really enjoyed this movie and had a fun time with it. I like how this remake wasn't just a complete copy and paste story of the original movie. They swiftly establish the lore and cover Pamela Voorhees' story in the opening credits which I really appreciate because whilst Pamela is the OG killer, with this franchise, everybody wants to see Jason . Also, the birth of the iconic hockey mask is shown nicely here. One of the most memorable things about this remake is that it doesn't waste any time getting to the action and kills and it sustains this energy throughout the movie. The opening sequence is one of the best I've ever seen in a horror movie. Just that sequence alone would make for a great Friday The 13th short film. It's absolutely brutal and incredibly effective. The rest of the movie continues like this. The kills are so brutal and gloriously nasty, especially that opening sleeping bag kill. Derek Mears as Jason Voorhees is probably my favourite portrayal of Jason in the franchise. He's brutally terrifying, aggressive and monster-like throughout the movie. I also like how this Jason is smart and adaptable. His whole underground tunnel system is pretty clever and it explains how he's able to get around so quickly. I will admit that the writing is very cheesy and sometimes just straight up silly and it can be a bit distracting from the fun, darker tone but it doesn't really bother me too much. Also, I think a lot of people's biggest problem with this film is just how annoying and cliche the characters are. But I think that works for this movie and I mean, have the characters in this franchise ever really been that likeable? Overall, this Friday The 13th remake is a really underrated and incredibly brutal entry in this iconic franchise. With the cliche characters, silly dialogue, brutal kills, cool lake house location and Jason going into full monster mode, this movie fully embraces Jason's cult iconography. It's just a damn shame that this never got a sequel and nearly 20 years later, we still haven't gotten a new entry to this iconic franchise.

Friday the 13th (2009) was my first experience with the franchise, and honestly, I had a great time with it. It doesn’t try to reinvent the slasher genre, but it knows exactly what it wants to be, and it delivers an entertaining ride from start to finish. Clay was easily my favorite character. Unlike many slasher protagonists, he isn’t just trying to survive—he’s determined to find his missing sister, and I loved how he never gave up on her. I also appreciated how protective he was of Jenna, which made him someone I genuinely rooted for. Trent was easily my least favorite character. His arrogance and attitude made him impossible to like, so his fate felt well deserved. I also liked that Jason wasn’t portrayed as a completely mindless killer. He follows a distorted logic shaped by his obsession with his mother. Whitney survives because she reminds him of her, which helps explain his actions—but it never excuses them. Understanding a villain’s motives is very different from justifying their crimes. The film doesn’t introduce anything particularly new to the slasher formula, but I honestly didn’t mind. I enjoyed it for what it was, and as my first Friday the 13th film, it definitely made me interested in the franchise. Sometimes a classic formula is all you need when it’s executed with confidence.
